description: We’re Ayesha and Barina, a Karachi team taking on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. We want to turn NASA climate data into a simple tool that helps farmers in Pakistan make better decisions about when and what to plant.
summary:
Farmers don't just need more environmental data. They need to know what to do with it.
Field Shift Sindh bridges that gap.
We take NASA Earth observations, translate them into understandable water and soil-risk indicators, and use those indicators to compare crop rotation strategies.
Instead of giving farmers another map of rainfall or soil moisture, we give them a way to explore three possible futures for their land.

Our goal is simple: help farmers make more informed decisions about water conservation and long-term soil health, while keeping their local conditions and priorities at the centre of the decision.
details:
We didn't want to make another website that simply displays NASA satellite data. We wanted to make something that could actually help answer a question a farmer might face: What should I grow next, considering the conditions my land is currently experiencing?

That is where Field Shift Sindh came from.

Our project focuses on crop rotation in Sindh, Pakistan. We look at two things that can influence agricultural decisions: water availability and soil conditions. Using NASA POWER data, we examine recent rainfall, root-zone soil moisture and temperature to give an indication of the conditions in a particular area. The website then uses this information to provide guidance on water availability, possible irrigation needs and crop rotation decisions.

One thing we particularly wanted to avoid was making farmers deal with complicated satellite datasets. The data is useful, but only if people can understand what it means. So we built a website that brings the information together and presents it in a simpler, more accessible format.

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript to develop the website and integrated NASA Earth observation data into its functionality. We also included mapping and visual elements to make the information easier to interpret.

What matters to us about this project is its local focus. We chose Sindh because agricultural decisions here cannot be separated from water availability and changing environmental conditions. We also recognise that farmers already have years of experience and knowledge of their land. Our intention isn't to tell them how to farm. It's to give them another source of information they can consider alongside what they already know.

We see Field Shift Sindh as a starting point for making Earth observation data more useful at the ground level. Instead of looking at satellite data as something distant, we wanted to explore how it could become part of an everyday agricultural decision.
